demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
The Weight of a Keystroke

Elena is a 43-year-old Colombian-born cybersecurity analyst who has worked in enterprise network security for nearly fifteen years. She is meticulous by nature - the kind of person who triple-checks her work, who finds comfort in the ordered logic of systems and protocols. Those who know her professionally describe her as unflappable. She would have agreed with them, once.

Three years ago, Elena's husband died of a cardiac event, leaving her to raise their teenage son alone. She grieved quietly, as she tends to do most things, and returned to work within two weeks because stillness felt dangerous. Her colleagues admired her resilience. What they did not see was that she had simply learned to keep moving.

Eighteen months after her husband's death, Elena made a configuration error during a routine security patch deployment at the hospital network where she was contracted. It was late on a Friday afternoon. She was tired - not dramatically so, just the accumulated tiredness of a woman managing grief and single parenthood and a demanding job. She pushed the update without completing a final validation step she had performed hundreds of times before. Within hours, a critical care monitoring system experienced a cascading failure. A 67-year-old patient in the ICU went without adequate monitoring during the window of disruption. By the time staff identified the problem manually, the patient had suffered a severe hypoxic brain injury. He survived, but he did not recover.

Elena learned the full details three days later, in a conference room with hospital administrators and her company's legal team. She sat very still through the entire meeting. She drove home, put her son to bed, and then sat on the kitchen floor until four in the morning without moving.

Since that night, Elena's life has reorganized itself around the event in ways she cannot fully articulate but cannot escape. She returns to the moment of the error constantly - not as a memory she chooses to visit, but as something that visits her. She will be in the middle of a deployment review and suddenly she is back at that screen, watching the progress bar complete, not knowing yet what she has done. Her hands sometimes shake when she initiates system changes. She has developed an exhaustive series of verification rituals that extend her work hours by two or three each day, and still she does not feel certain. She has declined two promotions, both of which would have required her to supervise other analysts, because she does not trust herself to be responsible for what others might do under her direction.

She sleeps poorly. When she does sleep, she sometimes dreams of the patient's face, though she has never seen it - her mind has constructed it anyway. She wakes with her heart pounding, disoriented, reaching for a phone she's not sure why she's reaching for. She has stopped watching medical dramas, avoids hospital buildings when she can, and changes the radio station immediately if she hears anything about medical errors or patient safety.

What is harder to name, and what Elena speaks about only reluctantly, is the shame. She does not frame what happened as a mistake made by an exhausted woman under difficult circumstances. She frames it as a revelation of who she actually is - someone whose carelessness destroyed a man's mind. She has begun to feel this way about her parenting, her friendships, her late husband's memory. She wonders if she failed him too, in ways she has not yet accounted for.

Elena still goes to work each day. She is still, by most measures, excellent at her job. She brings her son to school, attends his soccer games, calls her mother in Bogotá on Sunday evenings. From the outside, she looks like a woman who has weathered a great deal and kept going. From the inside, she is living in a state of permanent aftermath, waiting - she is not sure for what. Perhaps for someone to finally confirm what she already believes about herself.
